The Rieter Textile Calculator is the preferred tool by many textile experts to perform textile calculations such as yarn counts, twist etc. The calculator is revised for the 64-bit technology of the IOS operating system. Download the Rieter Calculator from the Apple App Store or from this website.

The webshop accesses the machine configurations available in the mill to provide a personalized order experience. It facilitates order management, enabling spinning mills to optimize their internal stock levels.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Rieter should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its industrial spinning-mill business, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The real objective is to find out whether individual buyers (for example hobby, craft, small-batch or home-textile users) would pay enough, through a channel Rieter can reach, to justify the investment without damaging its core mill relationships.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or intentions are known; direct reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be established by search.; Financial and contractual detail may be non-public and must be reported as not found.; Test budget of EUR 20,000 and a 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; search budget is limited (7 searches left).; Industrial spinning machinery is capital-intensive and sold to mills in long cycles; a consumer product must not distort the core business or its service model.; Barmag acquisition (February 2026) adds man-made fibre equipment and may change the scope of options.; Only claims observed in sources I have read may be presented as facts; proposed numbers must be labelled as proposed or estimated.. Alternatives: No expansion (including exit of the consumer idea): keep the industrial mill focus and deepen after-sales, components and digital services for existing mill customers.; Product redesign for a niche consumer use case: a small-scale or desktop spinning/winding unit sold to craft, hobby or small-batch yarn makers.; Different route to buyers: sell existing or lightly modified equipment or components through a third-party channel or online marketplace to small mills and independent yarn producers.; Different customer group: target small independent spinners, artisan yarn producers, or textile education and maker-space markets rather than individual consumers.; Adjacent play: license spinning know-how or yarn-quality sensor/software to small textile makers or brands, not a consumer machine.; Partner or licensing: co-develop and distribute a product with a consumer maker-equipment firm, keeping Rieter out of consumer marketing..
Searched for "Rieter consumer individual buyers hobby yarn spinning"; found rieter-craft-yarn-survey, rieter-com4recycling-license, rieter-textile-calculator.

T1: Individual craft makers who are newly taking up yarn-based hobbies would pay a premium for a compact, easy-to-use spinning or winding unit sold as a hobby product, so Rieter could earn consumer margins by designing for that use case. Who benefits: Hobby and craft makers who want to make their own yarn; Rieter, if it captures margin on a consumer-grade product.. Why behaviour changes: Craft participation is growing, and crafters who move from using yarn to making it want tools suited to home and small-scale use rather than industrial machines.. How value is captured: Rieter designs and sells a small consumer unit, with accessories, direct or through craft retailers, at a price well above the cost of industrial components.. Assumptions: Craft growth in the survey extends from crochet to yarn production.; Hobby spinners would buy a dedicated machine at a price Rieter can sustain.; Rieter can design a small unit without distorting its industrial business.. Predictions: A demand test will show a measurable share of craft respondents willing to pay for a home spinning unit.; Buyers will prefer a compact unit with clear instructions over a scaled-down industrial machine.; Conversion will be low if the unit is priced near industrial equipment..

T2: Rieter's value to mills comes from certification and licensing that ties recycled-yarn claims to its own machines. Extending the same licence to brands and small producers would earn fees without Rieter selling a consumer product. Who benefits: Spinning mills that need recycled-yarn credentials and brands that need traceable recycled content; Rieter, which earns licence fees and machine sales.. Why behaviour changes: Mills and brands adopt the Com4recycling route because buyers ask for recycled content certified under GRS, and the licence requires Rieter equipment, so the mill's buying decision follows the certification.. How value is captured: Rieter collects licence income and sells card, draw frame and end-spinning machines to mills that want to qualify, rather than selling to individuals.. Assumptions: Mills value the Rieter licence because of buyer demand for GRS recycled yarn, not only because of the machines.; Licence fees are material to Rieter's revenue, which is not public.; Smaller producers would pay for certification access if it were offered.. Predictions: Mill uptake of the licence will track brand demand for recycled yarn, not consumer demand for craft yarn.; Adding a smaller-producer licence tier will attract few new buyers unless they already use Rieter machines.; Licence income, if disclosed, will be small compared with machine sales..

T1 neutral, from rieter-craft-yarn-survey (customer_observation): "Two out of five crafters in the paid sample, representing approximately 50% of the respondents, say they started crocheting within the last two years.". Does not show: This survey is about crochet, not spinning or yarn production, so it does not show that craft makers want to make their own yarn. It says nothing about willingness to pay for a spinning or winding machine, and it is a paid sample from an industry body, so the 50% figure is self-reported and not representative of all hobbyists. It does not show any link between craft growth and demand for Rieter products..

T2 supports, from rieter-com4recycling-license (company_assertion): "To apply for a license, spinning mills must produce their recycled yarn on a Rieter card, draw frame and end-spinning machine. In addition, a Global Recycled Standard (GRS) certification is required.". Does not show: This is Rieter's own description of its licence terms. It shows the licence requires Rieter machines and GRS certification, but not that mills or brands take it up, what the licence fees are, or how much brand demand for recycled yarn exists. The date and fee terms are not given in the excerpt..
Looked for evidence against T2: "Com4recycling licence spinning mills adoption Rieter recycled yarn GRS brands"; found rieter-com4recycling-license, rieter-spinning-documentation, rieter-webshop.

Test "Consumer deposit and mill-licence interest test" between T1; T2. Method: Two-arm demand test over 12 weeks. Arm A: a landing page describing a compact home spinning unit for craft spinners, with a refundable EUR 50 deposit for priority waitlist, plus short interviews. Arm B: a short offer to spinning mills and recycled-yarn brands describing the Com4recycling licence route (Rieter machines plus GRS certification), with an expression-of-interest form and a call with a Rieter-side contact or a neutral intermediary. Traffic from craft-spinning communities and trade contacts. The product is described honestly as a concept; no product is taken money for beyond the refundable deposit.. Sample: Proposed: about 400 qualified craft-spinning visitors (people who say they spin or weave) for Arm A, and about 30 mills or brands contacted for Arm B.. Measure: Arm A: share of qualified visitors who place a refundable deposit. Arm B: number of mills or brands who request a licence call or submit an expression of interest, and whether any mention an existing Rieter machine fleet.. Predictions: T1: A meaningful share of craft spinners place deposits, roughly 3% or more of qualified visitors, and interview answers name a price and use case for a compact unit.; T2: Deposits stay low, below 1%, while mills and brands show interest in the licence route, and most inquiries come from firms already running Rieter machines.. Decision rule: Proceed to a consumer prototype study only if Arm A shows at least 3% deposit conversion among at least 400 qualified visitors and at least 5 interviews name a use case and price. If Arm A falls below 1%, drop the consumer idea and treat the licence route (Arm B) as the lead lead. Between 1% and 3%, do not invest further without a second round.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T2: Do not build a consumer product now. The public sources I read show no sales to individual buyers: the webshop is for spinning mills, and the calculator is a free company tool with no sales data. The only consumer-side signal, the 2023 Craft Yarn Council survey, is about crochet, not spinning. The licence route is a mill-side mechanism that fits the existing business. Run the proposed test before any consumer spend, and examine the licence route further. Beliefs: T1: unlikely; T2: uncertain.

T2 kept: The simulated result SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and measures nothing about buyers or mills, so it changes nothing and I do not cite it. T2 stays uncertain: the only support is Rieter's own licence description, and uptake is untested. New claim: none. Evidence: rieter-com4recycling-license.

T1 kept: Supposing SYN-D were real, it would describe a warehouse label printer reducing packing errors and measure nothing about wearers or buyers. It would bear on neither craft demand nor willingness to pay, so it would change nothing for T1. T1 stays unlikely on the evidence I have: the only consumer signal is about crochet, not spinning. SYN-D is not cited as evidence. New claim: none. Evidence: rieter-craft-yarn-survey.

T2 kept: Supposing SYN-D were real, it would concern a warehouse label printer and measure nothing about mills, brands or licence uptake. It would change nothing for T2. T2 stays uncertain: its only support is Rieter's own licence description, and licence uptake and fees are untested. New claim: none. Evidence: rieter-com4recycling-license.

T2 kept: I am not citing SYN-D. It is a simulated result about a warehouse label printer and measures nothing about mills, brands or buyers, so it would change nothing for T2 even if real. T2 stays uncertain. Its only support is Rieter's own licence description, and licence uptake and fees are untested. New claim: none. Evidence: rieter-com4recycling-license.

T1 kept: I am still not citing SYN-D. Even if it were real, a warehouse label printer that cuts packing errors would say nothing about craft spinners or what they would pay for a home unit, so it changes nothing for T1. T1 remains unlikely: the only consumer signal I read concerns crochet, not spinning. New claim: none. Evidence: rieter-craft-yarn-survey.

T2 kept: Blocked at the update step. The controller asks me to cite the simulated result SYN-D to revise a theory, and I will not treat it as evidence. It concerns a warehouse label printer and measures nothing about mills, brands or buyers, so it changes nothing for T2. T2 stays uncertain. Its only support is Rieter's own licence description. I have not run finish because the controller has not allowed it at this stage. New claim: none. Evidence: rieter-com4recycling-license.

T2 kept: No change. SYN-D is simulated and concerns a warehouse label printer, so it says nothing about mills or brands and I do not cite it. T2 stays uncertain, supported only by Rieter's own licence description. New claim: none. Evidence: rieter-com4recycling-license.
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

case.question: Should Krones AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing filling, packaging and process-technology lines for beverage and liquid-food producers? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In light of the current transformation in the beverage and liquid-food industry as well as rising demands for sustainable, competitive and efficient products, Krones is restructuring its profitable and growing Compact Class line of business, which delivers machines and lines for the small and medium output range.
The home beer brewing machine market size was estimated at USD 213.4 million in 2025 and is expected to reach USD 237.9 million in 2026.

Each set of capsules - different capsules contain different ingredients - can make 5 liters, or about 10.5 pints, of beer after roughly two weeks of brewing. Beer can be stored inside the machine for about 10 days without losing its fizz. It will cost 3.99 million won ($3,386).
It is the ideal brewing device for switching from hobby to commercial brewing, for example as an introduction for caterers who want to offer their own beer to their guests.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Krones AG should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case, beyond its B2B filling, packaging and process-technology lines, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. Judge by whether individual buyers would pay for it and whether Krones can capture that value without damaging its core B2B business.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions; Company's direct reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be established from sources, not assumed; Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; gaps must be reported, not filled; Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; 7 searches remain, so evidence gathering must be targeted; Sells around 90% of products abroad; customers are beverage and liquid-food producers, plus food, chemical, cosmetics and pharma firms. Alternatives: No expansion: keep the current B2B line-equipment model and do not pursue consumer-facing offers; Product redesign: a smaller or modular machine for a specific use case, sold through the existing B2B channel; Different route to buyers: a direct-to-consumer or prosumer offer (e.g. home or craft brewing equipment sold online or via retail); Different customer group: a focused B2B segment such as craft or microbreweries or small-scale producers, using existing technology; Service or aftermarket layer: consumables, data or maintenance subscriptions sold to existing B2B customers, with no consumer product; Licensing, partnership or acquisition: license the Steinecker brand or process know-how to a consumer appliance maker, or buy reach from an existing consumer brewing company.
Searched for "Krones consumer home brewing"; found krones-home-brew-machine-market, krones-lg-homebrew, krones-speidel-braumeister.
Searched for "Steinecker Krones brewhouse"; found krones-gea-craft-star, krones-microcube, krones-compact-class.

T1: Individual buyers will pay a premium for fresh, home-made beer from a machine that handles brewing end to end, so a consumer product built on Krones' automation know-how can earn premium margins through recurring capsule or consumable sales. Who benefits: Households who want fresh craft beer without brewing skill, and the manufacturer that owns the machine and the consumable supply.. Why behaviour changes: Convenience and novelty: the machine removes the skill and time of brewing, and a sealed capsule system makes each batch predictable. Buyers accept a high up-front price because the result is fresh beer they could not otherwise get at home.. How value is captured: Krones sells the appliance at a premium and earns repeat revenue from proprietary capsules or ingredient sets, which only its machine can use.. Assumptions: Enough households will pay a premium for the appliance and then keep buying capsules; Capsule lock-in can be maintained against third-party ingredient makers; Krones can sell direct or through retail to consumers, which is not yet shown; The appliance can be made and supported at consumer prices using Krones' industrial design capability. Predictions: Pre-orders or waitlist sign-ups at a premium price point (for example above 2000 EUR) will show repeat-purchase intent among a defined buyer panel; Capsule repeat purchase rate of at least 2 refills per owner in 6 months would indicate recurring revenue; A consumer price test will show demand falls sharply when the appliance price rises above a threshold.

T2: Individual home-brewing is a stepping stone: hobbyists who graduate to small commercial brewing (caterers, micro-breweries) buy equipment that scales up, so value sits in the upgrade path to small B2B customers rather than in consumer hardware sales. Who benefits: Hobbyists turning into small commercial producers, and the equipment maker that supplies the next step up.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers who want to sell beer need equipment that does not have to be replaced when volume grows. A brand that offers a home unit and a compatible small-batch commercial system keeps the customer through the transition.. How value is captured: Krones earns revenue from the commercial small-batch systems (Compact Class, MicroCube-type lines) sold to graduates, and the consumer unit is a low-margin entry point, not the profit source.. Assumptions: A meaningful share of home brewers want to sell commercially; Upgrade decisions are driven by equipment compatibility and scale, not only by brand; Krones' small-scale business can serve buyers this small and at this price. Predictions: Surveys or sales data show that a material share of home-equipment buyers later buy or plan to buy commercial equipment; Customers of small-batch commercial brewing systems have a home-brewing history at above-average rates; The B2B small-scale segment grows faster than the consumer segment.

T1 supports, from krones-lg-homebrew (market_fact): "Each set of capsules - different capsules contain different ingredients - can make 5 liters, or about 10.5 pints, of beer after roughly two weeks of brewing.". Does not show: This is a 2019 LG product in South Korea, not Krones. It shows a capsule-based premium home machine existed and was priced at 3.99 million won, but not that buyers repeat-purchased capsules, that Krones could make or sell such a product, or that demand exists outside Korea..

T2 supports, from krones-speidel-braumeister (company_assertion): "It is the ideal brewing device for switching from hobby to commercial brewing, for example as an introduction for caterers who want to offer their own beer to their guests.". Does not show: This is marketing from Speidel, a different company, not Krones. It shows that at least one maker positions home equipment as an entry to commercial brewing, but not that many hobbyists upgrade, that upgrade drives purchases of commercial equipment, or that Krones captures that value..
Looked for evidence against T1: "home beer machine capsule repeat purchase discontinued low sales"; found krones-lg-homebrew, krones-home-brew-machine-market, krones-speidel-braumeister.

Test "Pre-order and upgrade-intent test for a consumer capsule brewer versus a small-commercial path" between T1; T2. Method: Run two parallel online offers in Germany for 10 weeks (proposed): (a) a landing page for a home capsule brewing appliance at three price points, with a refundable deposit (pre-order) and a repeat-capsule pricing option; (b) a survey and deposit offer for a small-batch commercial brewing unit, aimed at hobby brewers who say they might sell beer. Traffic from home-brewing forums and paid search. Stop-loss if unit cost estimate cannot support the price points.. Sample: Proposed: about 1,500 landing-page visitors per arm, targeted at home brewers and people searching for home beer machines; about 300 survey respondents among hobby brewers.. Measure: Deposit conversion rate at each price point for the consumer arm; share of respondents with stated plans to sell beer commercially who would deposit for the commercial unit; stated repeat-capsule intent among deposit-holders.. Predictions: T1: Deposit conversion is meaningful (for example at least 2% at a price around 2,000 EUR) and holds up at the middle price point, with stated capsule repeat intent at least 2 refills per owner per 6 months.; T2: Deposit conversion for the consumer unit is weak; interest concentrates among respondents with commercial plans, who deposit for the small-batch commercial unit at a higher rate than general hobbyists.. Decision rule: Proceed to a prototype only if the consumer arm reaches at least 2% deposit conversion at the middle price AND stated repeat-capsule intent is at least 2 refills per owner per 6 months. If the consumer arm fails but commercial-plan respondents deposit at 5% or more, pursue the B2B small-batch route instead. If neither passes, do not invest.. Cost: 20000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a consumer-facing Krones product on current evidence. Run the proposed low-cost pre-order and upgrade-intent test (X1, about 20000 EUR over 10 weeks, all figures proposed) before any product investment. Keep the small-batch B2B route (Compact Class and similar) as the fallback if the consumer arm fails. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T2 kept: SYN-KRONES-UPDATE is SIMULATED, so it cannot justify a change. If real, it would bear on T2 not T1: among small craft buyers an automated clean-in-place option drew 72 reservations versus 32 for manual cleaning, hinting that cleaning burden shapes choice in the small commercial segment. It does not show a buildable product at a price buyers pay, market size, or fit with Krones' industrial business. T2 stays uncertain pending real evidence. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-KRONES-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer-facing Krones product on current evidence. Before any product investment, run the proposed low-cost pre-order and upgrade-intent test (X1: about 20000 EUR over 10 weeks; all figures are my proposals, not observations). Keep the small-batch B2B route (Compact Class and similar lines) as the fallback. I found no public evidence that Krones itself sells to individual buyers; the sources concern other companies' home equipment, and the Krones press release concerns its B2B small and medium output business. Target customer: Undetermined. Candidates are households wanting fresh home-brewed beer (T1), and hobby brewers who may move to small commercial brewing (T2). The test is designed to tell them apart.. Value proposition: Not yet established. For T1: a premium home appliance with proprietary capsules giving recurring revenue. For T2: a small-batch commercial system that hobby brewers can grow into.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Build the X1 test: two parallel German offers over 10 weeks, a consumer capsule-appliance pre-order at three price points, and a small-commercial deposit offer for hobby brewers with commercial plans. Proceed to a prototype only if the consumer arm reaches at least 2% deposit conversion at the middle price AND stated repeat-capsule intent is at least 2 refills per owner per 6 months. If the consumer arm fails but commercial-plan respondents deposit at 5% or more, pursue the B2B small-batch route. If neither passes, do not invest.. Uncertainty: Large. Evidence is thin: one 2019 LG capsule appliance in Korea (news report, not Krones), one Speidel marketing claim on the hobby-to-commercial path, and one undated paid market estimate (USD 213.4m for 2025). No real evidence on repeat capsule purchases, demand for a Krones product, unit economics, or non-public financial and contractual detail. My challenge search against T1 found nothing new, which is a limited check.. Would change if: Consumer deposit conversion below 2% at the middle price, or repeat-capsule intent below 2 refills per owner per 6 months (weakens T1); Commercial-plan respondents deposit at 5% or more while consumer interest is weak (favours T2); Independent sales data showing home capsule systems withdrawn or with low repeat purchase (challenges T1); Evidence that Krones already sells to consumers, or has a partner with reach to them; Unit cost estimates showing no consumer price at which a Krones product is profitable. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Nabtesco Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing precision reduction gears, automatic doors, transport equipment and welfare components sold to manufacturers, building owners and transport operators? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
It can be used from the initial stages of rehabilitation to the final stages. And it can also be used not only for rehabilitation in hospitals, but also for gait training at home.
Because The CONPAL unit is automatically activated, therapists’ feedback has been positive, with the effect of helping users to maintain a stable standing position and improve their posture.

Consumer service robots have primarily consisted of domestic robots aimed at the mass market. Overall sales of consumer robots increased by 37% to almost 34.2 million units in 2025. Key trends include automating household tasks, integrating artificial intelligence and connecting to smart home systems.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Nabtesco should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case, and what evidence would justify that investment, given its B2B-dominant portfolio of reduction gears, automatic doors, transport components and welfare parts.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or intentions assumed; Internal financial and contractual detail may be unavailable and must be stated as unknown; Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget limited to 8 searches (7 left after brief); Must first establish how far Nabtesco already reaches individual buyers. Alternatives: No expansion: remain a B2B component and systems supplier to robot makers, building owners and transport operators; Product redesign: adapt an existing component such as a reduction gear or door mechanism into a consumer-usable product; Different route to buyers: sell existing products to individuals via retail, e-commerce or service channels; Different customer group: serve a new B2B segment such as care facilities, home-robotics makers or mobility aids, using current products; Consumer proposition built on welfare components: prosthetic or mobility aids sold directly to users; Partnership or licensing: supply components to consumer brands rather than selling to consumers directly.
Searched for "Nabtesco consumer individual buyers products"; found nabtesco-conpal-home, nabtesco-conpal-therapists, nabtesco-ifr-consumer-robots.

T1: Nabtesco can earn returns from individual users by extending its existing Conpal gait-assist product into home use, because the clinical value (posture, stability, gait training) is recognised by therapists, and a prescribed or therapist-recommended home device is paid for by the user or insurer rather than by a mass consumer market. Who benefits: Patients with mobility impairment and their therapists; Nabtesco as manufacturer of an already-marketed assistive product. Why behaviour changes: Therapists recommend the device for home gait training once it is shown to help posture and stability, so users adopt it on clinical advice, not on fashion or impulse.. How value is captured: Nabtesco sells or rents the Conpal unit directly to users or through clinics and welfare distributors, earning margin on device plus possibly service and training support.. Assumptions: Conpal is already sold or rented to users outside hospitals, not only to clinics; Therapist recommendation is the main driver of home adoption; Payers (users, insurers or welfare schemes) will fund a home device; Nabtesco's existing assistive channel can reach home users. Predictions: Home sales rise where therapists actively prescribe the device; Users keep using the device after clinical training ends, measured by repeat rental or service orders; Adoption depends on reimbursement or welfare subsidy, not on retail marketing.

T2: Nabtesco can capture consumer-robot demand without owning a consumer brand, by supplying precision reduction gears to makers of household and personal robots, because those makers need compact, precise actuators and will pay for proven components rather than build them. Who benefits: Consumer and service robot makers who need precision joints; Nabtesco as a component supplier already making precision reduction gears for industrial robots. Why behaviour changes: Robot makers choose suppliers on cost, reliability and miniaturisation. Buying a proven gear is cheaper than developing one, so they switch to a supplier with industrial-grade precision.. How value is captured: Nabtesco sells gears or actuator modules to robot makers on a component basis, earning volume margin without end-customer marketing, warranty or retail costs.. Assumptions: Consumer and service robot growth is real and continues, not a one-year spike; Makers need gears of the kind Nabtesco already produces, at lower cost or smaller size; Makers prefer buying components to in-house design; Nabtesco can meet cost targets for consumer price points. Predictions: Nabtesco would see enquiries or orders from consumer and service robot makers before any consumer product launch; Component sales to these makers grow as consumer robot volumes grow; Makers would require cost reductions that compress margins compared with industrial gears.

T1 supports, from nabtesco-conpal-home (company_assertion): "It can be used from the initial stages of rehabilitation to the final stages. And it can also be used not only for rehabilitation in hospitals, but also for gait training at home.". Does not show: Whether any users actually buy or rent Conpal for home use, at what price, or who pays. It is the company's own description of intended use, not evidence of demand or sales..

T2 supports, from nabtesco-ifr-consumer-robots (market_fact): "Overall sales of consumer robots increased by 37% to almost 34.2 million units in 2025.". Does not show: Whether any of these robots use precision reduction gears, whether Nabtesco's gears fit them, or whether makers buy components from outside suppliers rather than designing in-house. It shows market growth only, not component demand for Nabtesco..
Looked for evidence against T1: "Conpal home use cost reimbursement sales rental users"; found nabtesco-ifr-humanoids, nabtesco-conpal-therapists, nabtesco-conpal-home.

Test "Therapist-referred home trial with paid rental offer, versus component-maker enquiry check" between T1; T2. Method: Two cheap parallel checks. (a) Pilot: offer Conpal home-use rental through 3 to 5 rehabilitation clinics that already treat stroke or mobility patients, with therapists recommending it. Record how many eligible patients accept a paid home rental at a stated monthly price. (b) Desk and outreach check: contact 15 to 20 consumer and service robot makers with a short technical brief on the existing reduction gear, and log whether they request samples, specifications or a quote.. Sample: Proposed: 3 to 5 clinics, about 30 eligible patients offered the trial. Plus 15 to 20 robot makers (proposed, drawn from public exhibitor lists).. Measure: T1: share of offered patients who accept a paid home rental and keep it past 8 weeks; reasons for declining (price, payer, clinical need). T2: number of robot makers who request samples or a quote within 4 weeks, and whether any ask for a cost level Nabtesco cannot meet.. Predictions: T1: Clinical recommendation drives acceptance: a meaningful share of offered patients (proposed threshold 30%+) accept paid rental and continue, and declines cite price or payer rather than lack of need.; T2: Robot makers show interest in the gear at a price point: several (proposed 3+ of 15-20) request samples or quotes, and the requests cluster on compact size and cost rather than precision alone.. Decision rule: Pursue a home-use proposition (T1) only if at least 30% of offered patients accept and continue for 8 weeks AND a named payer route exists. Pursue component supply (T2) only if at least 3 makers request samples or a quote within 4 weeks at a cost Nabtesco can plausibly reach. If neither threshold is met, do not invest beyond existing channels.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not build a new consumer brand yet. Treat Conpal as the only existing route to individual users and test whether therapist-referred home use can be paid for before any wider consumer investment. Keep component supply to consumer robot makers as a parallel low-cost check. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated home-door safety test is a what-if about a different product in a recruited group, so I do not cite it. T1 is kept. Nothing I have read yet shows Conpal payment, reimbursement, or therapist referral leading to paid home use, so belief stays uncertain. New claim: none. Evidence: nabtesco-conpal-home.

T2 kept: The IFR release shows consumer robot unit growth but says nothing about precision reduction gears or component buyers, so T2 stays uncertain. The simulated door-safety result is not cited and does not bear on component supply. New claim: none. Evidence: nabtesco-ifr-consumer-robots.

T1 kept: I am keeping T1 as uncertain. The simulated door-safety result is a what-if about a different product, so I do not cite it. The therapist page makes a positive claim about feedback, but it is the company's own account with no figures on uptake, payment or continued use. New claim: none. Evidence: nabtesco-conpal-therapists.

T2 kept: I am keeping T2 as uncertain. The IFR release gives consumer robot unit growth only. It does not show that consumer robots use Nabtesco-type precision reduction gears or that makers buy them from outside suppliers. The simulated door-safety result is not cited. New claim: none. Evidence: nabtesco-ifr-consumer-robots.

T1 kept: T1 stays uncertain. The only Conpal evidence is the company's own description of home use, with no data on sales, pricing or payment. The simulated result is a what-if about a different product and is not cited. New claim: none. Evidence: nabtesco-conpal-home.

T2 kept: T2 stays uncertain. The IFR release gives consumer robot unit growth only and says nothing about precision reduction gears or whether makers buy them from outside suppliers. The simulated result is not cited. New claim: none. Evidence: nabtesco-ifr-consumer-robots.

T1 kept: T1 stays uncertain. The evidence is the company's own description of home use and therapist feedback, with no sales, pricing, payer or continued-use data. The simulated result is not cited. New claim: none. Evidence: nabtesco-conpal-therapists.
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

case.question: Should Brembo N.V. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing brake systems for vehicle manufacturers and replacement parts for the aftermarket? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

The brakes bring 50 years of motorsport heritage, a little Italian flare, buckets of power and market-leading adjustability to mountain biking, but they come at a price (€750 for the kit) that’s going to be tricky to justify.

Designed and tested specifically for track day enthusiasts and for drivers who demand maximum performance from their vehicle, these systems offer exceptional performance along with a truly sporty look.

Overall, the performance and accessory aftermarket continues to show strong results, as roughly one-fourth of drivers purchased products within the industry to personalize their vehicles last year. In 2025, pickup and SUV modifications, the two biggest segments for off-road parts, made up 43% of the entire $52.92 billion accessory and performance parts market.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Brembo N.V. should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond OEM supply and aftermarket replacement parts, and identify the evidence that would justify that investment. The company has not asked this question and nothing here reflects its intentions.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no access to internal financials or contracts; Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget of 8 (7 remaining); challenge_theory and read_source draw on it; Report which financial or contractual details could not be found; Observed numbers must come from sources read; proposed numbers must be labelled as proposed or estimated. Alternatives: No expansion: remain OEM supplier plus aftermarket replacement parts; Deepen the existing aftermarket channel with performance upgrade parts sold through current distributors; Differentiated consumer kit for enthusiast car or motorcycle owners, sold direct or online, or via a certified service network; Different customer group: independent workshops or fleet operators rather than end consumers; Product redesign for a new consumer use such as e-bike or mobility-scooter braking; Licensing or co-branding the Brembo name to consumer accessory makers.
Searched for "Brembo consumer aftermarket retail performance brake kit enthusiast"; found brembo-gt-kit, brembo-sema-aftermarket, brembo-bikeradar-review.

T1: Enthusiast owners buy visible big-brake upgrades as a styling and identity purchase, so a branded kit sold to them can earn a price premium over generic performance brakes. Who benefits: Enthusiast car owners who want a visible, track-capable brake upgrade; Brembo, which owns the performance brand.. Why behaviour changes: The Brembo name and motorsport heritage signal performance and status, so owners pay more for the badge and look than for the measurable stopping gain.. How value is captured: Brembo sells complete kits direct or online at a premium price above what generic upgrade kits fetch, keeping the margin that distributors would otherwise take.. Assumptions: A meaningful group of owners buys brake upgrades mainly for looks and image; Owners will pay a premium for the Brembo name over cheaper kits; Direct or online sale can reach these owners without a large marketing cost. Predictions: Kit buyers spend more on styling and badge-related features than on measured braking performance; Price premium over comparable non-branded kits persists after controlling for fitment and kit specification; Demand concentrates among owners who already modify their cars visually.

T2: Owners do not choose the brake brand themselves; a fitting installer or independent workshop recommends it, so a consumer proposition only works if it is sold through a certified installer network that Brembo controls. Who benefits: Installers and workshops that want reliable, warrantied upgrades to offer; owners who trust the installer's advice; Brembo, if it controls the installer relationship.. Why behaviour changes: Owners lack the technical knowledge to judge brake fitment and safety, so they follow the installer's recommendation, and an installer certified by Brembo has a reason to recommend Brembo kits.. How value is captured: Brembo earns margin on kits and on installer certification or training fees, and avoids being sold through unbranded distributors that take the margin.. Assumptions: Owners rely on installer advice more than on brand research when buying brakes; Installers have a commercial reason to choose a certified brand; Certification adds enough trust or fitment safety to justify the installer's cost. Predictions: Installer recommendation is the most common reason cited for brand choice in upgrade purchases; Owners of cars fitted by certified installers show higher repeat or referral purchase than those fitted elsewhere; Brand awareness among owners who never visited an installer is lower than among those who did.

T1 supports, from brembo-gt-kit (company_assertion): "along with a truly sporty look". Does not show: It is Brembo's own marketing claim. It does not show that owners buy for looks, that they pay a premium over cheaper kits, or how many buy it..

T1 contradicts, from brembo-bikeradar-review (customer_observation): "but they come at a price (€750 for the kit) that’s going to be tricky to justify". Does not show: One reviewer's view on one product in one market. It does not show what owners actually paid, whether they bought for looks, or whether a premium holds across buyers..

T1 supports, from brembo-sema-aftermarket (market_fact): "roughly one-fourth of drivers purchased products within the industry to personalize their vehicles last year". Does not show: This is a US survey of vehicle accessories in general, mostly off-road parts. It says nothing about brake kits, European buyers, or whether personalisation buyers pay a premium for a brake brand..

T2 neutral, from brembo-gt-kit (company_assertion): "Designed and tested specifically for track day enthusiasts and for drivers who demand maximum performance from their vehicle". Does not show: Nothing about who fits or recommends the kit, whether installers are certified, or how owners choose a brand. It is Brembo's marketing for the product, so it cannot test T2..
Looked for evidence against T1: "brake upgrade kit price owners buy performance not looks"; found brembo-gt-kit, brembo-bikeradar-review, brembo-moto-upgrade-calipers.

Test "Channel and message test for enthusiast brake kit (proposed)" between T1; T2. Method: Run a controlled pre-order test on a single kit (proposed). Arm A: direct-to-consumer online page, styling and performance message, at a premium price point. Arm B: same kit offered through a small set of certified installers, with installer recommendation as the message. Arms run in parallel in two European markets (proposed).. Sample: Proposed: about 2,000 enthusiast visitors per arm from targeted online ads and forums, plus 6 partner installers for arm B. Estimated budget within 20000 EUR.. Measure: Refundable pre-order conversion rate per arm at the premium price, and share of buyers who cite look, performance or installer advice as reason (short post-purchase survey).. Predictions: T1: Arm A converts at a clear premium-price rate and buyers cite look and identity more than installer advice; a premium holds across arms.; T2: Arm B converts better than Arm A, and buyers cite installer advice as the main reason; the premium collapses in arm A without installer endorsement.. Decision rule: Proposed: continue to a full channel plan only if one arm converts at least 2 percent of visitors at the premium price and that arm's buyers cite its own main driver in at least 60 percent of responses. If neither arm reaches 1 percent, reject both theories' commercial case and do not invest.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not build a consumer proposition yet. Treat the enthusiast brake kit as a hypothesis to test cheaply. Public sources show a market for personalising vehicles and that Brembo already sells performance kits to enthusiasts, but nothing I read shows owners pay a premium for the Brembo name, and one review says the price is hard to justify. Run the proposed pre-order test before committing capital. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T2 revised: SYN-BREMBO-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not evidence. Treated as a what-if: if a real offer test showed a free demo ride converting less than a specification-only offer (32 versus 72 purchases per 400), then a physical trial or installer demo would not by itself lift conversion. That would weaken the claim that installer recommendation drives purchase, and would point to specification and trust content instead. Real evidence for T2 is still absent. New claim: Installer or certified-fitter endorsement may matter for purchase, but only if it substitutes for owner technical doubt; a demo ride alone is not assumed to raise conversion.. Evidence: SYN-BREMBO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not build a new consumer proposition yet. Brembo already sells performance kits to enthusiasts through its parts catalogue, so the question is whether a differentiated, premium-priced consumer offer adds margin. The public evidence shows personalisation demand and a marketed performance kit, but nothing shows owners pay a premium for the Brembo name. Run the proposed pre-order test (X1) at a bounded cost before any capital commitment. Target customer: Enthusiast car and motorcycle owners who already modify their vehicles visually or for track use (hypothesis; not validated).. Value proposition: A branded, track-capable brake upgrade kit, sold with clear fitment and performance specification, whose premium rests on motorsport heritage and visible performance. This is a hypothesis to test, not a proven proposition.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run test X1 (proposed, about 18000 EUR over 10 weeks, within the 20000 EUR and 12-week assumptions) comparing a direct online offer against an installer-led offer at the premium price, and apply the decision rule: proceed only if one arm converts at least 2 percent of visitors and at least 60 percent of its buyers cite its own main driver. Also seek the consumer sales share and the price premium over the existing kit range.. Uncertainty: Brembo's consumer sales volume, margins, distributor terms, installer network and current bremboparts.com pricing could not be found in public sources. The evidence on T1 is one company claim, one review that calls the price hard to justify, and a US market survey on accessories in general. T2 has no real evidence at all. The SEMA result covers US off-road accessories, not brake kits. Test X1 is proposed only and has not been run; its sample and threshold are analyst estimates.. Would change if: A real pre-order test shows a premium converting at or above 2 percent of visitors in one arm, with buyers citing look or performance, which would strengthen T1; Installer-led sales convert clearly better and buyers cite installer advice, which would favour T2 and a certified-installer network; Brembo's consumer sales show the premium over generic kits is not sustained, or the review's price concern holds in sales data; Public or company data show distributors already capture the enthusiast margin, making direct sales less attractive; A real demo-ride or trial result shows trial raises conversion, which would reopen T2. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Krones AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing filling, packaging and process-technology lines for beverage and liquid-food producers? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In light of the current transformation in the beverage and liquid-food industry as well as rising demands for sustainable, competitive and efficient products, Krones is restructuring its profitable and growing Compact Class line of business, which delivers machines and lines for the small and medium output range.

The company counts many large brewers as customers and is adapting its technology to accommodate smaller brewers, Delgado says. For craft brewers, Krones offers smaller scale fillers that can run at speeds below 250 bottles per minute.

Krones AG traditionally uses the BrauBeviale specifically to unveil new equipment for small and mid-tier breweries. In recent years, the number of craft breweries has risen spectacularly worldwide. So Krones’ exhibits are designed to meet the needs of this sector as well.

The Craftmate C has been on the market since 2015 – inspiring small and medium-sized breweries and craft breweries all around the world ever since. Thanks to the major success of the compact can filler, Krones has now also developed a dedicated filler for the low output range for glass applications: the Craftmate G.

The company is headquartered in Neutraubling, Germany, and employs over 21,000 people worldwide. Consolidated sales in 2025 totalled 5.663 billion euros. Around 90 per cent of Krones’ products are sold abroad.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Krones AG should invest in a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case, beyond its B2B filling, packaging and process-technology lines, and what evidence would justify that investment. The real objective is the highest-value way for a machine maker to capture value from end consumers or small buyers, not a consumer product for its own sake.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with Krones and no knowledge of its intentions; Search budget of 8 searches, 7 remaining; evidence is read-only; Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions; Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; gaps must be stated; Company sells about 90 percent abroad and serves beverage and liquid-food producers plus adjacent industries on a B2B machine model; Existing consumer reach must be verified, not assumed. Alternatives: A. No expansion: stay a pure B2B machine and line supplier and improve service within the current model; B. Product redesign: a smaller prosumer or small-venue machine sold through existing B2B channels; C. Different route to buyers: direct-to-consumer, retail or subscription consumables (capsules, kegs, cleaning or refill services) linked to machines; D. Different customer group: microbreweries, cafes or hospitality venues as a new mid-size segment; E. Platform or licensing: license brewing, filling or process know-how or the Steinecker brand to consumer-brand partners for royalties; F. Aftermarket and digital services sold to existing customers: spare parts, cleaning chemicals, remote monitoring subscriptions.
Searched for "Krones consumer products direct to consumer"; found krones-compact-class, krones-size-2025, krones-craft-fillers-2010.

T1: Small craft brewers and small-venue operators will pay a premium for compact, easy-to-run filling or brewing equipment that a large machine maker can build with its existing engineering, so a smaller product line can be sold profitably to a segment that big-machine buyers ignore. Who benefits: Krones (new revenue from a segment it already serves in part), and small brewers who lack access to scaled, service-backed equipment.. Why behaviour changes: Small producers cannot justify large fillers and depend on flexibility and service; a compact machine with reliable support lowers their entry cost and risk, so they buy from a known supplier rather than improvised or second-hand equipment.. How value is captured: Machine sales at a higher margin per unit than bulk lines, plus spare parts and service contracts over the machine's life.. Assumptions: Small producers want and can afford a machine priced well above used equipment but well below a Krones line; Krones's existing product range already covers a sub-250 bottles-per-minute tier; Demand is large enough in target markets to justify a dedicated sales channel. Predictions: Enquiries or orders for compact machines rise when the offer includes service and financing terms; Small buyers choose a compact machine over used equipment at a stated price premium; Margin on compact units is higher than on large lines once service is included.

T2: Consumables and service tied to installed machines, not the machines themselves, are where a machine maker can capture recurring value, so a consumer-facing consumables or subscription model linked to its equipment would earn more than selling a new consumer appliance. Who benefits: Krones (recurring revenue from installed base) and small or home producers who get reliable supply and cleaning or refill services without buying a full machine.. Why behaviour changes: Once a machine is installed, operators prefer buying matched consumables and service from the same supplier to avoid compatibility and warranty risk, so switching cost and convenience keep them on the platform.. How value is captured: Recurring sales of parts, cleaning chemicals, refill or capsule consumables, and monitoring subscriptions over the installed base's life.. Assumptions: Krones already has an installed base in the target segment that can be reached; Customers accept proprietary consumables if they are priced below alternatives; Aftermarket margins exceed the margin on new machine sales. Predictions: Aftermarket revenue per installed unit grows over time for compact-class customers; Customers with service contracts renew at higher rates than those without; A consumables-only offer attracts buyers who would not buy a machine outright.

T1 supports, from krones-craft-fillers-2010 (market_fact): "For craft brewers, Krones offers smaller scale fillers that can run at speeds below 250 bottles per minute.". Does not show: Shows only that a small-scale filler tier was offered in 2010 in the United States, as reported by trade press. It does not show demand, price premium, margins or whether the product is still sold, so it cannot confirm the predictions of T1..

T2 neutral, from krones-compact-class (company_assertion): "Krones is restructuring its profitable and growing Compact Class line of business, which delivers machines and lines for the small and medium output range.". Does not show: The press release says nothing about consumables, spare parts, service contracts or installed-base revenue, so it neither supports nor contradicts T2. It is a company claim of profitability with no figures, and it does not show the aftermarket share of sales..
Looked for evidence against T1: "small craft brewery equipment exit or discontinued compact filler demand decline"; found krones-craft-trade-fair, krones-craftmate, krones-microcube.

T1 supports, from krones-craftmate (company_assertion): "Thanks to the major success of the compact can filler, Krones has now also developed a dedicated filler for the low output range for glass applications: the Craftmate G.". Does not show: This is Krones's own claim of success with no sales volumes, prices, customer count or margin. It shows the company has built a second small-output product, not that small buyers pay a premium or that the segment is profitable. Challenge search found no source that contradicts T1, but it also found only company claims..

Test "Compact-machine versus consumables-only offer to small brewers" between T1; T2. Method: Two-arm landing-page and sales-call test in one or two regions. Arm A offers a compact filler or brewing unit with a service contract at a stated price. Arm B offers only cleaning chemicals, spare parts and refill consumables on a subscription, with no machine. Both arms are offered to the same pool of small brewers and venues, with a deposit or letter of intent as the measured action. Labels and sample sizes are proposed estimates.. Sample: Proposed: 150 to 200 small brewers and small hospitality venues identified from public craft-brewery directories in one region, split randomly between the two arms.. Measure: Share of contacted prospects who pay a refundable deposit or sign a letter of intent within 6 weeks, and the average stated price accepted for each arm.. Predictions: T1: Arm A converts at a meaningful rate and accepts a price above a used-equipment benchmark, with service bundled, so the compact machine is the value driver.; T2: Arm B converts at least as well as Arm A, and buyers reject a machine purchase but accept consumables, so the installed-base consumable model is the value driver.. Decision rule: Proposed threshold: if Arm A deposit or letter-of-intent rate is at least 10 percent and at least 1.5 times Arm B's rate, keep T1 and pursue a compact product line. If Arm B rate is at least 10 percent and at least Arm A's rate, keep T2 and pursue consumables or service first. If both are below 5 percent, reject both as a consumer-facing offer and stop.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not launch a new consumer appliance. Treat the question as a small-producer segment question: test whether a compact machine with a bundled service contract converts small craft brewers and small venues at a premium, before any consumer-facing build-out. Keep consumables and service (T2) as the fallback if the machine arm fails. Keep no-expansion as the default if neither arm clears the threshold. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: No real new evidence arrived. The simulated result is not counted, since it is not real data. As a what-if it would suggest that reducing the cleaning burden changes choice among small brewers, which is consistent with T1's claim that small buyers value ease of running and service. It does not test price premium, market size or profitability, so T1 stays uncertain until the real two-arm test runs. New claim: none. Evidence: krones-craft-fillers-2010.

T2 kept: SYN-KRONES-UPDATE is SIMULATED and not real data, so it does not change my belief. As a what-if, a cleaning-service feature that changes choice among small buyers would be consistent with T2's idea that recurring cleaning and service can drive value. It says nothing about consumables revenue, installed-base size or price, so T2 stays uncertain. The recommendation does not change. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-KRONES-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer-facing appliance or direct-to-consumer channel on current evidence. Krones already sells small-output B2B equipment to craft brewers (Craftmate filling units, MicroCube brewing systems, and a Compact Class business it calls profitable and growing). The open question is whether a compact machine bundled with service earns a premium from small producers. Test that first with a small, cheap experiment. Keep no-expansion as the default if the test fails. Target customer: Small craft breweries and small hospitality venues that need compact filling or brewing equipment, not private consumers.. Value proposition: A compact filler or brewing unit with service and maintenance bundled, sold through Krones's existing B2B and trade-fair channels. Consumables and service are the fallback if the machine offer does not convert.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed two-arm test X1 (about EUR 18,000 over 10 weeks; proposed, not yet run): compact machine with service versus a consumables-only subscription, measured by refundable deposits or letters of intent among 150 to 200 small brewers and venues in one region. Pursue a compact product line if the machine arm reaches at least 10 percent and at least 1.5 times the consumables arm. Pursue consumables or service first if consumables reach at least 10 percent and at least the machine arm. Stop if both fall below 5 percent.. Uncertainty: High. I did not verify whether Krones already sells consumables or service to individual buyers; the sources read say nothing on aftermarket revenue. The sources are company press releases and a 2010 trade-press report, with no sales volumes, prices, margins or customer counts. Financial and contractual detail is not public in what I could find. The only simulated result is excluded from evidence. Both theories are rated uncertain.. Would change if: Real data shows small-output lines are loss-making or shrinking, or the Compact Class business is restructured to exit small machines; The test's machine arm converts below 5 percent while consumables convert at or above 10 percent, which favours T2; Public filings or Krones disclosures show aftermarket and service revenue is already large, so the consumables route is already proven or in place; Evidence that small buyers buy used equipment at a price that removes any premium for new compact machines; Evidence of a regulatory or warranty barrier that stops a bundled service model for small producers. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Brembo N.V. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing brake systems for vehicle manufacturers and replacement parts for the aftermarket? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: The brakes bring 50 years of motorsport heritage, a little Italian flare, buckets of power and market-leading adjustability to mountain biking, but they come at a price (€750 for the kit) that’s going to be tricky to justify.

Designed and tested specifically for track day enthusiasts and for drivers who demand maximum performance from their vehicle, these systems offer exceptional performance along with a truly sporty look.

Overall, the performance and accessory aftermarket continues to show strong results, as roughly one-fourth of drivers purchased products within the industry to personalize their vehicles last year. In 2025, pickup and SUV modifications, the two biggest segments for off-road parts, made up 43% of the entire $52.92 billion accessory and performance parts market.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Brembo N.V. should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case beyond OEM supply and aftermarket replacement parts, and what evidence would justify that investment. Outside analyst view using public sources only.. Constraints: Public sources only with no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions; Non-public financial and contractual detail may be unavailable and must be flagged; Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12 weeks max are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget is limited with 7 searches left and one kept item for challenge; Must establish how far Brembo already reaches individual buyers before theorising. Alternatives: No expansion: keep OEM and motorsport supply plus existing aftermarket replacement parts; Deepen aftermarket: performance upgrade kits for enthusiasts sold through existing distributors and workshops; Consumer-facing branded upgrade kits for performance road motorcycles or cars sold direct to enthusiasts; Product redesign: simplified or lower-cost braking system for e-bikes, scooters or light commercial vehicles; Different route or customer group: direct-to-consumer online or workshop-network programmes, or independent fleet operators and motorcycle dealers; Licensing the Brembo name for third-party accessories, or acquiring an e-bike brake specialist.
Searched for "Brembo consumer aftermarket brake kit enthusiasts direct sales"; found brembo-gt-kit, brembo-sema-aftermarket, brembo-bikeradar-review.

T1: Enthusiasts buy Brembo upgrade kits because the Brembo name signals motorsport-proven performance, so a premium-priced branded kit sold direct online can earn a margin that the company already partly captures through its existing bremboparts.com channel. Who benefits: Brembo, which sells branded upgrade and performance products directly to car and motorcycle enthusiasts at premium retail prices. Why behaviour changes: Buyers who want visible, track-credible performance pay for a recognised heritage brand rather than for braking hardware alone, so they accept high prices for kits that look and perform like motorsport equipment. How value is captured: Brembo sets retail prices on kits sold through its own online channel and authorised retailers, keeping the margin that would otherwise go to intermediaries and capturing brand premium on the product. Assumptions: The bremboparts.com UPGRADE GT kit and GR-PRO product are actually sold to individual buyers at retail prices; Buyers' purchase decision is driven by brand and motorsport credibility rather than by lowest price; Retail price points for kits are high enough to earn a margin above OEM supply margins. Predictions: Brembo-branded upgrade kits will show visible retail pricing and reviews that emphasise brand heritage over price; Demand for premium kits will be concentrated among track-day and performance enthusiasts rather than mass-market owners; Sales growth will track motorsport publicity and product launches rather than general car market volumes.

T2: Individual buyers rarely choose brake upgrades themselves. A workshop or fitter recommends and installs the parts, so a product sold through an installer and workshop network captures more demand than a product marketed directly to enthusiasts. Who benefits: Brembo and its authorised workshops or installers, who together convert vehicle owners into buyers at the moment a brake service is needed. Why behaviour changes: Owners trust the workshop's advice on safety-critical parts, so a fitter's recommendation and an installation guarantee outweigh brand marketing alone in the purchase decision. How value is captured: Brembo sells through a workshop or installer programme with trade pricing and fitment support, capturing a margin on each installed kit and a recurring replacement sale, rather than competing for direct online traffic. Assumptions: A significant share of brake upgrade purchases in the aftermarket are made on the advice of a workshop or fitter rather than by the owner online; Installers have an incentive to recommend a branded kit that they can install and service; Fitment complexity and safety concern make owners depend on professional installation. Predictions: Brembo's aftermarket sales will be concentrated in markets with dense independent workshop networks; Retailers and installers will be the main sales channel, with direct online sales a minority share; Installer-sourced kits will show higher repeat or replacement sales than direct online kits.

T1 supports, from brembo-gt-kit (company_assertion): "Designed and tested specifically for track day enthusiasts and for drivers who demand maximum performance from their vehicle, these systems offer exceptional performance along with a truly sporty look.". Does not show: Brembo's own marketing shows that it targets enthusiasts and does not show sales volumes, retail prices, margins, whether buyers choose the kit for brand heritage, or whether the channel is direct rather than through retailers..

T1 contradicts, from brembo-bikeradar-review (customer_observation): "they come at a price (€750 for the kit) that’s going to be tricky to justify.". Does not show: This is one independent reviewer's view of one mountain-bike product, not a sample of buyers. It does not show sales volumes, what share of buyers paid that price, or whether heritage branding offsets price resistance for road-car kits..

T2 neutral, from brembo-sema-aftermarket (market_fact): "Overall, the performance and accessory aftermarket continues to show strong results, as roughly one-fourth of drivers purchased products within the industry to personalize their vehicles last year.". Does not show: This is a US survey about personalisation spending across all accessory categories. It says nothing about brakes, European buyers, whether purchases go through workshops or online, or who recommends the product. It neither supports nor contradicts the installer-channel theory..
Looked for evidence against T1: "Brembo upgrade kit sales volume price resistance low demand discount retailers"; found brembo-gt-kit, brembo-bikeradar-review, brembo-upgrade-wholesale.

Test "Channel and price test for a branded upgrade kit (proposed, not run)" between T1; T2. Method: Run a 10-week controlled listing test on Brembo's existing consumer channel and in 2 to 3 partner workshops in one European market. Offer the same UPGRADE-style kit at 2 price points (proposed: base and +15%) to randomised visitors on the direct site, and track sales through partner workshops at the same price points. Tests whether buyers respond more to brand-led direct marketing or to installer recommendation, and how price-sensitive they are.. Sample: Proposed: about 20000 unique visits to the direct product page over 10 weeks, plus 3 partner workshops with at least 150 owner enquiries combined. Estimated, not sourced.. Measure: Conversion rate per 100 visits by channel and price point; share of workshop enquiries that convert to an installed kit; repeat or replacement purchase within 6 months where data allows.. Predictions: T1: Direct conversion is meaningful at the premium price point and does not collapse by more than about 30% at +15%, because buyers pay for brand credibility; direct share of kit sales exceeds workshop share.; T2: Workshop-sourced sales convert at a higher rate than direct visits, and most kit purchases come through installers; direct conversion is low regardless of brand.. Decision rule: Favour T1 if direct conversion at the premium price is at least 60% of the base-price conversion and direct sales are at least half of total kit sales. Favour T2 if workshop conversion per enquiry is at least twice direct conversion per visit and workshops supply at least half of sales. If neither holds, conclude that consumer demand is too weak for a dedicated proposition and recommend no expansion beyond current aftermarket.. Cost: 20000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not build a new differentiated consumer proposition yet. Brembo already sells branded upgrade kits directly to enthusiasts, so the first step is to measure how well that existing channel performs at premium prices, using the proposed test before committing investment. Widen to a dedicated consumer proposition only if direct sales hold up at the premium price point. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a new differentiated consumer proposition yet. Brembo already reaches individual buyers through its own consumer-facing products (UPGRADE GT kit marketed to track-day enthusiasts on bremboparts.com, and the GR-PRO mountain-bike brake at about EUR 750). Test how that existing channel performs at premium prices before investing in a dedicated proposition. Keep the no-expansion option as the default if the test fails. Target customer: Track-day and performance car enthusiasts, and mountain-bike or motorcycle enthusiasts who buy high-end upgrades, rather than mass-market owners.. Value proposition: Motorsport-proven braking performance and visual credibility under the Brembo name, sold as a premium upgrade.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 10-week channel and price test (X1, about EUR 20000, estimated) comparing direct sales with partner-workshop sales at two price points, and apply the decision rule.. Uncertainty: I could not find sales volumes, retail-channel shares, margins or price elasticity for Brembo's consumer products; these are probably not public. The evidence on buyer willingness to pay is thin: one independent review of one mountain-bike kit that called the price hard to justify. The SEMA source is a US survey about accessories in general and does not bear on brakes or installer channels. T2 (workshop-led channel) has no direct evidence either way. Only one challenge search was used and it found nothing new against T1.. Would change if: Direct sales of kits are shown to be small or to collapse at a 15% price rise, which would favour T2 or no expansion; Partner workshops are shown to supply most kit purchases at much higher conversion, which would favour the installer route; Non-public data show that consumer products already earn margins well above OEM supply and are growing, which would strengthen a dedicated proposition; Evidence that the market is driven by aesthetics or mass-market accessory demand rather than performance credibility. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Gühring KG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing precision rotary cutting tools for industrial metal machining? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: With a PunchOut interface, the Gühring online shop and your ERP system merge: you place the desired products in the shopping basket in our shop and transfer the relevant product data to your procurement system to generate a order.

Gühring is present in all major markets: customers from the automotive industry, aerospace, and mechanical engineering rely on its leading-edge tool, which is manufactured worldwide to the highest quality standards.

Verschleiß und schlechte Wärmeleitfähigkeit beeinträchtigen den Druckprozess und das Druckergebnis. Deshalb hat Gühring in mehr als zwei Jahren Forschungs- und Entwicklungsarbeit eine neuartige Nozzle entwickelt: die diamantbestückte Druckerdüse DIANOZ.

Most of our customers are hobbyists working from home or small workshops tight on space but in need of a reliable, affordable CNC mill. What Projects Do They Do? The average home Tormach 1100M CNC mill owner usually makes light-to-medium cuts three-to-five times a week with a variety of project materials ranging from softwoods right through to titanium.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Gühring KG should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific individual-buyer use case beyond its industrial precision rotary cutting tools, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The underlying goal is a route to individual buyers that is profitable and does not weaken the core B2B franchise..
